newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end broadly lower as rate worries worsen.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end broadly lower as rate worries worsen.

text.p: Stocks fell sharply on Wednesday, amid mounting interest rates pressures and an intensified sell-off in technology shares.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 45.79 points to 7,039.37, after falling more than 70 points earlier. The drop ended a string of two record closing highs of 7,085.16 on Tuesday and 7,079.39 on Monday.
In the broader market, losers beat winners 1,566 to 934 on heavy volume of 483.1 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
The broad sell-off took the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks and Nasdaq Composite indices down by nearly one full percent.
Beyond the technology sector, the stiffest selling seemed directed toward financial and pharmaceutical stocks, which have posted the sharpest rallies this year.

The Philadelphia Stock Exchange's Bank index fell 10.90 points or 1.70 percent, to 629.64, while the American Stock Exchange's Pharmaceutical index fell 6.99, or 1.66 percent, to 414.55. Drug giant Merck & Co. Inc. was among the weakest Dow components, falling 1-5/8 to 92-1/4.
During the latest gains by the Dow, investors were clearly unwilling to broaden stock picks beyond mainly defensive blue chip issues, undermining the large-cap rally, analysts said.
"Bull markets don't scream ahead when defensive names are in the leadership," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
"With the market as fragmented as it is, we'll have very significant problems making headway and be subjected to substantial profit-taking at the high end of our trading range," he said.

Interest rates continued creeping up, as the bond market remained nervous about inflation even though a closely watched Federal Reserve report released Wednesday showed price pressures are under control.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 11/32, or $3.4375 on a $1,000 bond, which raised its yield to 6.88 percent from 6.85 percent at Tuesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

In its Beige Book report on U.S. economic conditions, the Fed described price pressures as "temperate." Likewise, wage gains remain moderate and show no signs of spiking higher despite tight labour markets, it said.
The news temporarily cheered financial markets, triggering a brief recovery in both stocks and bonds. But the sense of caution that has gripped the market of late quickly returned.

"I didn't see anything, frankly, that would be a smoking gun for a tightening by the Fed," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "But I think everyone on the planet knows they're going to tighten and it's just a question of when and by how much."
For now, analysts said, the interest rate issue offers a welcome opportunity to cash in on some of the latest gains for blue chips.
Among individual issues, OfficeMax Inc. rose 1-5/8 to 15 after announcing it agreed to buy 63 stores from Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. for about $109 million.

Following news of the sales, the Federal Trade Commission said it would meet with Staples and Office Depot to reconsider the commission's opposition to their planned merger. Office Depot shares jumped 3-5/8 to 23 but Staples fell 1-1/4 to 22.
General Signal Corp. fell 3-1/4 to 40-3/8 after the company warned that its first-quarter earnings would be below year-ago levels.
Marsh & McLennan Cos Inc. gained 7 to 129. The company said it will acquire privately held insurance broker Johnson & Higgins for a $1.8 billion combination of stock and cash.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 12.63 points to 1,304.13.
The S&P 500 index fell 7.08 points to 804.26.
The American Stock Exchange index was off 1.39 to 602.04.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 3.52 to 423.54. The average price per share fell 37 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,675.292, down 65.862, or 0.85 percent.
